title: The right amount of stress
text: Stress is usually discussed as poison, but the oldest {{1}} in psychology says otherwise. In 1908, two researchers {{2}} that performance on any task rises with arousal — alertness, pressure, excitement — up to a point, and falls away {{3}} it. Too little stress and we are {{4}}; too much and the same arousal that sharpened us begins to scatter attention and {{5}} memory. The curve matters most where stakes and skill interact. Beginners {{6}} under pressure and do best in calm; experts, whose skills run on automatic, often need the opposite — the boxer who feels nothing before a fight worries his corner more than the one who cannot sit still. The practical {{7}} are refreshingly ordinary: rehearse enough that the task itself feels easy, treat the racing pulse as fuel rather than {{8}}, and remember that the goal is not a stress-free life but the right dose at the right moment. Butterflies, as the old performers' saying has it, are fine. You just have to make them fly in formation.

gaps.explanation: 'the oldest law in psychology' — the Yerkes-Dodson law; lore = traditional knowledge, flaw = a defect.
'two researchers demonstrated that…' — showed it experimentally; denominate = name in a unit.
'falls away beyond it' — past that point; the image is a curve with a peak that performance drops after.
'too little stress and we are sluggish' — slow and underpowered; snappish = irritable.
'scatter attention and impair memory' — damage it; impart = give or communicate.
'beginners wobble under pressure' — lose steadiness; waffle = talk vaguely, wrench = twist violently.
'the practical takeaways' — the points to take away and apply; takeover = acquiring a company.
'as fuel rather than menace' — something to use, not to fear; massage = kneading the body.
